What Would Roland Emmerich Do? BY JODY DUNCAN n 1996, director Roland Emmerich and producer Dean Devlin brought to the big screen Independence Day, a story in which an outgunned but determined humanity defends itself against an invasion of technologically advanced aliens. The movie grossed more than $800 million at the box-office, transformed Will Smith from television to movie star, and seared images of beloved landmarks being blown to smithereens into the brains of audiences worldwide. Given the spectacular success of the film, a sequel should have followed as surely as night follows day; but no sequel was forthcoming in the years following the release of Independence Day, despite 20th Century Fox's eagerness for it. Roland wasn't into doing sequels of his movies," recalled visual effects supervisor Volker Engel, who cut his teeth on the 1996 project, and went on to collaborate with Emmerich on a number of films. "He was much more interested in doing something completely different. Several years later, I recall that he said, 'Never say never, but I'd have to come up with a really good idea to do an Independence Day sequel.'" 1 / 33 Having come up with that really good idea, Emmerich and Devlin entered into prelim-

INDEPENDENCE DAY inary negotiations with Fox in 2010. In 2014, the filmmakers presented Fox with 17 key images from the proposed film - as rendered by Trixter art director Luis Guggenberger and his team of six artists - securing the studio's greenlight. iOur job was to develop Roland's vision for the movie," related Trixter animation supervisor Simone Kraus, "and to help visualize it for the studio. We started a close collaboration with Roland, creating sketches for general framing and staging, and then continuing to finesse these 17 production paintings, step by step. Volker Engel provided us with references from the original film, and with those in mind, we created the key moments in the movie in these Photoshop type images, which we then combined with 3D elements in a photoreal stylei With the project now greenlit, Emmerich, Engel and their teams began preproduction on Independence Day: Resurgence. First on the agenda were designs for the aliens and their ships, initial versions of which were rendered by Aaron Sims Company. Production designer Barry Chusid and his group of concept artists also began tackling the designs of many remaining assets, including a lunar base that would feature prominently. Later, the filmmakers hired artist and architect Johannes Mücke to design the alien mothership - which was so large, it was more a traveling continent than spacecraft - as well as the alien fighter, an alien queen's ship, a huge spherical ship from a new alien race and other assets. The 20-year gap between Independence Day and its sequel justified some modification to the designs, but not too much, as Emmerich wanted audiences to feel as if they had returned to the world of the first film.iWe wanted to respect everything that 2 / 33 had been done in the first movie," said Volker Engel, "so we considered these designs

to be a kind of 2.0 version of what we had already seen. It made sense that, after 20 years, the aliens would have updated their technology, just as we have. So the idea was to start with the basic design language that was developed for the first movie, but then take it to another level. The alien fighters, for example - which we called alien 'attackers' in the first movie - have a very similar look. They are larger, with some new elements, but they look as if they came out of the same alien factory." to get our core team back together again," said Engel, "which is really four main people: digital effects supervisor Marion Spates, compositing supervisor Ryan Smolarek, modeling supervisor Andre Cantarel, and animation supervisor Conrad Murrey. While Uncharted Territory would ultimately deliver 268 out of the film's 1,748 total effects shot count - making it the largest single effects contributor - the team started by generating previs, splitting the assignment with Deluxe's Method Studios. Among the key sequences the teams prevised was the alien mothership's arrival on Earth - a particularly challenging sequence to conceptualize, given that the ship was the size of North America, and would land with legs on both shores of the Atlantic Ocean. For a scene in which an alien queen's ship chases a school bus in the desert and then launches an attack on Area 51, Uncharted Territory went above and beyond traditional previs, running simulations and rendering images in Chaos Group V-Ray.We took INDEPENDENCE DAY s the design effort ramped up, Engel reassembled key members of Uncharted Territory, the longtime visual effects arm of Emmerich productions, whose business model has it folding between the director's projects. We were lucky enough 3 / 33

INDEPENDENCE DAY this previs to a higher level," recalled Marion Spates, "so Roland could tell the story better to the viewers at early test screenings." Pixomondo came on later to previs a handful of shots, and The Third Floor, Halon and Baraboom Studios also contributed previs later in production, when Uncharted Territory was taxed with producing its final shots. Production was based at Albuquerque Studios, where virtually the entire film was shot on partial sets, surrounded by bluescreen - Emmerich's preference, as it afforded him absolute control over lighting and protected the shoot from the elements and inconvenient sun angles. In addition to the stage sets, Barry Chusid built two outdoor sets representing parts of a compound belonging to an African warlord, which featured in only 40 shots. "We also had a couple of helicopter shots," noted Volker Engel, "with a jeep driving through what was supposed to be Africa, but was actually an outskirt of Albuquerque.i Emmerich also made a brief trip to Washington D.C. to shoot a suburban street. "Other than that, we were on indoor stages at Albuquerque Studios throughout." On the bluescreen stages, Marion Spates oversaw the use of Ncam's real-time camera tracking system, which enabled Emmerich to see, on his monitor, the digital aliens, ships, and environments that would be composited into scenes in postproduction. Working late at night and on weekends, modeling supervisor Andre Cantarel and his team had built low-res assets to be fed into the Ncam system in advance of the shoot, so they would be available from the beginning of principal photography. "It was tricky," noted Marion Spates, "because it wasn't just a matter of using our previs assets. Everything had to be built low-res, but with pre-baked lighting so it would look proper when Roland 4 / 33 saw it in the background." Typically, Ncam rigs were mounted on both the A and B cam-

INDEPENDENCE DAY eras. "We generally had two operating all the time. Ncam tracked the movement of those cameras, and then that data was sent back to a Motion Builder system, into which we'd fed all of the digital environments and assets. Spates often found himself animating digital characters or aircraft on the fly as Emmerich explored camera options on set. "For example," said Spates, "if there was a shot of the alien queen moving toward camera, I'd have to animate that right then and there, so the cameraman could tilt up and capture the queen in frame. It is hard enough to animate something like that, but, in this case, I was animating live to a moving camera. It was an intense setup - but Roland loved it, and he used it a lot." n postproduction, 16 visual effects companies worked collaboratively to deliver the film's effects shots, with visual effects art director Michael Maher contributing additional designs, as needed, and digital production supervisor Devon Patterson working with Volker Engel to ensure that art department concepts made their way into final visual effects shots, and that assets stayed 'on model' from one vendor to the next. Uncharted Territory served as the central hub of the global visual effects assignment. "Over the last several years," explained visual effects producer Marc Weigert, "Uncharted Territory has developed a project and asset management system that is centralized to the production. All of the meta-data - anything that gets collected from the set, assets, different versions of shots, and so on - resides in Shotgun, which is a production tracking software. But, Shotgun is in the cloud, and you don't want to have hundreds of tera5 / 33 bytes of data - or actual assets or shots - in the cloud. So we have built a bridge that

INDEPENDENCE DAY is comprised of a lot of different components, including the Vendor Transfer Tool. Every vendor installs that tool, which allows them to get all of the information directly from Shotgun. Then, on our side, Shotgun is directly connected with our own servers. So, a vendor can directly grab anything pertaining to their shots in Shotgun, using a download tool; then, they can submit shots to us, using the transfer tool, and the actual files get stored on our file system. Also, it gets automatically put on playlists and copied over into a screening room server, so we can look at it with the click of a button. ¿All of this is not necessarily glamorous or exciting, but it is very important. I have been a visual effects supervisor most of my life, and I learned early on that, as a creative person, you are 100% dependent on the managerial and fiscal aspects of a production. That's the reason we developed this system. We didn't want to waste time and money on bureaucracy that could have been used creatively." Uncharted Territory CG supervisor Andrew Roberts, in addition to overseeing some of the company's critical effects shots, coordinated the outsourcing and cloud rendering tasks. The efficient workflow proved critical to a project that was huge in scope, even by Roland Emmerich standards. After an opening one-minute shot flying through galaxies, nebulas and destroyed planets - an ominous precursor to the coming threat, created by Buf Studios - the first ten minutes of the movie, alone, feature enough spectacle, destruction and action for an entire feature. The film's story opens on the moon. Ironically, production crews drove through very lunar looking landscapes in the New Mexico desert on route to shooting a small terrain 6 / 33 set on stage at Albuquerque Studios. Awarded the moon sequence, MPC extended - and

INDEPENDENCE DAY ultimately replaced - the set digitally, matching NASA and Hubble Telescope photography. MPC also built a military defense base, erected on the moon in the 20 years since aliens first threatened Earth. ¿The majority of our shots took place on the moon base, which was like a city," said MPC visual effects supervisor Sue Rowe, "and so, we built that entire city. We did a lot of high-resolution 3D modeling for the base and the immediate area around it, and then we modeled lower-res areas beyond that. It took a long time, but it really paid off when it came to shot production, because it was just a matter of putting different cameras into our already established scene. That saved us time and gave Roland as much flexibility as possible." Early shots in the sequence reveal flying moon tugs - fueled by the alien technology left behind in the previous invasion - towing a massive cannon toward a nearly 1,000foot-tall, 400-foot-wide support tower. Crews shot actors in a practical 40-foot tug set, surrounded by blue. In addition to compositing in the surrounding landscape, MPC tracked in CG tug arms and mechanical fingers, which manipulate the cannon into place. MPC also replicated the entire tug in CG, using lidar scans and high-res photography of the practical craft. "That gave us a great start," Rowe stated. "We were able to replicate all the dents, scars and rivets that were on the set model on our CG model. Then, since it is powered by alien fuel cells, the moon tug - and all the vehicles in this movie - had the signature Independence Day green glow, indicative of the alien technology." For the cannon, MPC worked off art department designs. 'We didn't veer too far from those concepts," Rowe said, "but we added a lot of small-scale detail onto this enor7 / 33 mous structure, just to make it look more real and less CGi Working closely with Rowe

Whereas on Independence Day, aliens had been depicted primarily by performers in suits, the aliens in Independence Day: Resurgence were all-CG throughout, save for some practical tentacles provided by Fractured Effects for direct interaction between tentacle and actor. Image Engine, awarded all the alien shots - except for the alien queen revealed in the film's third act - started with concept models produced by Aaron Sims Company, but mostly relied on reference images of the Patrick Tatopoulos-designed aliens as they had appeared in the original film. "Matching the aliens in the first movie was the most important thing," said Image Engine visual effects supervisor Martyn Culpitt. "We added a bit more detail and texture in certain areas, but Roland wanted the audience to be able to connect this alien to the one in the first movie - at least in respect to the colonist alien." As in the first film, the colonist would wear an exosuit that was ultimately penetrated, revealing the more organic looking creature inside.iWe matched the looks of both the exosuit and the inner colonist alien." Image Engine also created a soldier alien. "We had a bit more leeway with that one," said Culpitt, 'and so, we added our own nuances, building on top of Aaron Sims' design. Somewhat similar to the colonist, the soldier alien is more rugged, with armor and a 8 / 33 cannon-like weapon that he carries; and, whereas the colonist stands about 91⁄2 feet tall,

the soldier is closer to 12 feet tall." INDEPENDENCE DAY To capture the base motions of the bipedal aliens, Image Engine used an Xsens mocap suit, which could record the wearer's actions anywhere - no mocap volume required. Someone could just walk around in this suit, and it would capture the motion through wifi, which was pretty cool," Culpitt commented. "All of the sensors were just there on the body, capturing the movement — the position of the wrist, the elbow, everything. The performer could walk up stairs, roll on the ground, and the suit would capture all of that. That gave us the base animation; and then our animation supervisor, Jason Snyman, designed a rig for animating movements that were more specific to the alien. Image Engine spent a full three months just developing the aliens' tentacle movement, which had been achieved practically in the first movie, with off-camera crews physically manipulating foam limbs. The more sophisticated CG tentacles in Independence Day: Resurgence would feature nuances and dynamics not possible in a practical setup. "We added a lot of dynamics to make it work," noted Culpitt. "Each tentacle inherited motion from the walk or the movement of the alien, and it also had its own rippling motion - so it got quite complex in the end.i Effects TDs set up the system so that animators could easily switch from keyframe animation to a procedural process, and back again. iA lot of it was procedural once we got the look that Roland liked, but we had to be able to switch from dynamics to actual interaction if a tentacle hit a wall or grabbed something.i Animators animated the tentacles in Autodesk Maya, with additional coding done in Image Engine's internal software. 9 / 33 Just as the imprisoned aliens begin to show signs of life, so too does an alien space- <

craft - a 'city destroyer' from the first film - that landed in a remote African village 20 years before. With work being done at both its Los Angeles and Vancouver branches, Scanline delivered 100 shots for the Africa sequence, for which the team digitally re-created the city destroyer built as a practical miniature in the original Independence Day. Scanline also did extensive environmental work for the sequence, extending a small village set built at Albuquerque Studios. prised of dozens of bays and hundreds of parked fighters - would be the setting of several sequences in the film. Production built a small section of one bay as a live-action set, but the remainder of the massive hangar was a CG environment created by Uncharted Territory. "All they had built was this façade that measured maybe 50 feet wide and 25 feet tall," noted Marion Spates. "They also had a lot of props on set, including a painted human fighter and a small buck for foreground fighters - but that was it. In the final shots, we see hundreds of rows of these fightersi Andre Cantarel was in charge of building the human fighter, which was then passed on to other vendors for their specific sequences. "The human fighter had the appearance of an F-22," commented Spates, "with alien technology engines placed on the axle, hanging off the wings." Once on the moon, fighter pilot Jake Morrison (Liam Hemsworth), on his iPad, reINDEPENDENCE DAY he action cuts to inside a huge hangar at Area 51, where a squadron of human fighter pilots assigned duty on the moon base is briefed. The gigantic hangar - measuring nearly 3,000 feet in length, and 1,500-plus feet in width, and com10 / 33 V

INDEPENDENCE DAY plays helmet camera footage of a flight accident that nearly cost the life of his best friend and fellow pilot, Dylan Hiller (Jessie Usher). Screen Scene delivered eight shots for the sequence, five of which involved blending a bluescreen element of Hemsworth sitting against a large window with a lunar background. More challenging was the witness camera imagery Screen Scene generated and composited into the iPad screen, which has Jake's fighter racing that of his buddy through the Grand Canyon, clipping his wing and causing his plane to crash into a canyon wall. To choreograph the fighters' flight and the subsequent collision and explosion, Screen Scene started with previs that had been created by Pixomondo, under Roland Emmerich's direction. "Roland likes to previs a sequence to within an inch of its life," Screen Scene visual effects supervisor Ed Bruce related, "and then hand it over, and say, 'Make that.' So that's what we did, initially. But when this sequence went through editorial, they edited the camera moves a bit, and chopped up the scene; and so, we had to re-choreograph our CG planes so that the timings all worked out to the story beats Roland required. Screen Scene artists used existing human fighter models, retexturing them in Autodesk 3ds Max to accommodate their specific shots, as well as existing digi-doubles and parachute assets for shots of Dylan ejecting from the explosion and parachuting toward the ground. Screen Scene created the Grand Canyon backgrounds racing past the fighters as a 3D environment, first building basic canyon geometry in 3ds Max, and then running that through a world generator to give it additional structure.iWe found that was good for I1 / 33 plotting a wider view," Bruce recalled, "and for giving us the shape and feel of a canyon

INDEPENDENCE DAY and its erosion; but it didn't give us the vertical detail that we needed for a canyon wall rushing very close to the side of the plane. So, we sculpted that extra detail in ZBrush. We also used a forest engine to scatter rocks and shrubbery around." The scene ends with the fighter exploding into a huge ball of fire, which Screen Scene created using Pflow and Fume within 3ds Max. Past calamities recede in the face of new threats, which first appear as a mysterious wormhole forms out of a lunar sandstorm, from which emerges a spherical spacecraft. An earlier version of the script had the alien mothership appearing out of a wormhole - an idea for which Trixter had spent considerable time and resources developing visuals. When the script was revised, the filmmakers took advantage of Trixter's headstart, awarding them wormhole shots now set on the moon. Emmerich's general directive to Trixter was to make the wormhole appear epic on screen. "He wanted it to have tremendous impact," commented Trixter visual effects supervisor Dominik Zimmerle. 'The concept art showed it as extremely complex, with many different structures and patterns. We ran fluid simulations to get these nice, oily, black parts, and composited roughly 30 layers - volume layers and point layers - to make up the wormhole." On orders from American President Lanford (Sela Ward), base personnel shoot down the sphere - only to learn that it was a ship of Artificial Intelligence beings intending to warn them of the malevolent aliens' imminent approach. Dr. David Levinson (Jeff Goldblum) and Jake Morrison then travel to the far side of the moon via moon tug to inves12 / 33 tigate the Al sphere crash site. "When the Al ship crashes," said Sue Rowe, whose MPC

team was assigned the sequence, "it creates these shards - like glass or eggshell pieces - forming a trench in the moon's surface. Our heroes land their moon tug and travel through this trench, surrounded by the alien crash site. For the crashed sphere itself, Emmerich asked MPC to create a kind of Russian Doll effect.iFrom the wreckage you see that the outside is made of a kind of carbon graphite surface. Inside of that is an exact replica; and inside of that is yet another replicai W ment. "This ship was our single biggest challenge," said Volker Engel. "There's a quote in the movie that sums it up: someone says that the mothership is descending over the Atlantic Ocean, and someone asks, 'Which part?' And the answer is, 'All of it.' So the problem was, how do you convey something of that size? It was easier when we were close to the ship because we could show all of the detail; but the moment we got further away from it, it was very difficult to convey the scale of this thing." 'The destroyers on the original Independence Day were about 18 kilometers in diameter, elaborated visual effects supervisor Bryan Grill, whose Scanline team would build the asset and then deliver shots of the mothership's arrival on Earth. 'This was almost 5,000 kilometers in diameter - a very big difference. All the texture on one of the original destroyers would cover only a tiny area of this thing. So scale, for us, was the biggest issue of the whole movie. It took months for us to wrap our heads around it. INDEPENDENCE DAY hile David and Jake investigate the crash site, the alien mothership - all 2,500 miles of her - approaches the moon. The sheer scale of the spacecraft was one of the most difficult aspects of the show's visual effects assign13 / 33

INDEPENDENCE DAY Just when we thought it was too big, Roland wanted it biggeri Rather than model the entire mothership in detail - a practical impossibility - Scanline built basic geometry and then detailed out only those areas that would feature in their shots. Scanline then turned over that basic geometry to other vendors, making it clear that they would have to detail areas of the mothership, as needed. MPC was among the vendors that took possession of Scanline's asset, which they detailed for shots of the mothership passing over and then clipping the moon. Among MPC's shots was a wide one revealing about three-quarters of the behemoth as it passes, with Earth in the background. "It is a classic Roland Emmerich shot," said Sue Rowe. "I remember looking at the previs of this shot, and thinking, 'Oh my God, how are we going to make that look good?' But I felt pretty good about it by the end. In total, MPC delivered 70 shots of the mothership clipping the moon's surface, causing massive destruction. MPC used its proprietary rigid body simulator Kali to generate the destruction effects, which grew in scope throughout postproduction. ¿This sequence took on a life on its own and got bigger and bigger, in true Roland Emmerich style, Rowe noted. So, there was a huge amount of work involved in it, with colossal moon rocks falling, and the fine powder of the surface being thrown up into the air. Rowe had been clued in to the epic scale of the final sequence when preparing shots of a rock hitting the moon's surface for the trailer. "I did three versions of it, and showed the biggest one to Roland, thinking that it was obviously too big. I said to him, 'I just put that in for scale reference.' And he said: 'No, that one's not big enough. I want it bigger!' After that, 14 / 33 on all our shots, we asked ourselves: 'Is it big enough for Roland Emmerich? What would

Roland Emmerich do?"" INDEPENDENCE DAY Moon base personnel fire the cannon at the mothership, but the beam is deflected by alien defense shields. The ship then brings out its big guns and fires on the cannon, destroying it. The massive explosion that follows was simulated, but was inspired by the look of the White House destruction in Independence Day. "We tried to mimic the look of that in this destruction shot," Rowe said. "Of course, in the first movie, it was a practical miniature, so it had a different look; but we used that shot as our inspiration for how we blew up the moon on this one The moon destruction is intercut with shots of President Lanford giving a speech in front of the Capitol building in Washington D.C. LUXX Studios in Stuttgart, Germany - which had generated a digital Washington D.C. for Emmerich's White House Down - built a futuristic version of the nation's capital for Independence Day: Resurgence, working from concepts that Emmerich had developed with Johannes Mücke and his team. At first," commented LUXX Studios producer and co-founder Andrea Block, "we were hoping that we could reuse about 40 to 60 percent of what we had built for White House Down, but we soon figured out that Roland wanted an absolutely new look. So we redesigned the Capitol building, and increased the scale of the Washington Monument and the city around it, which would show not only new business districts and skyscrapers, but would also be filled with Jumbotrons, moon tugs and aircraft boosted by alien technologyi "The idea," added visual effects supervisor Chris Haas, "was that everything had been destroyed in 1996, and when they built it up again, they tried to improve it. So, for 15 / 33 example, the Capitol is much bigger than before, because it has to fit all the people of

the alliance." The Washington Memorial, too, would be built as a larger monument, commemorating the victims of the 'War of '96.' While some of the structures were larger in the futuristic Washington D.C., the trees throughout the city were younger, and therefore smaller. Only the White House remains as we know it, the filmmakers reasoning that, if it had been destroyed, it would have been rebuilt exactly as it had been before, for purposes of continuity and sentimentality. director, Martin Wellstein, included sitting, clapping, idle motion, standing up, standing idle, waving, et cetera," said Andrea Block. "All of that motion-captured action was cleaned up by the animators and then arbitrarily placed in squadrons on the bleachers and in groups in front of the President. We also distributed hand-selected actions within the sections so that patterns wouldn't repeat themselves. Sometimes they were brushed up for frequency or amplitude to create a believable action overall." In the end, LUXX produced more than two hundred different people to create the crowd of 500,000. Later in postproduction, Emmerich asked that more people be positioned directly behind the President - close enough to camera to require facial movement in the CG crowd members. Since animating those facial movements wasn't doable in the allotted time, production set up a late shoot of extras to populate the near-camera crowd. 'The actions recorded by our technical 16 / 33 LUXX artists also contributed to other sequences, creating shots with futuristic air-

INDEPENDENCE DAY craft, hangars and airfields near Area 51, and a high-security bunker at Cheyenne Mountain. LUXX built 3D structures in 3ds Max, and composited them in Nuke. Most of Washington, the airfields and the bunker were 3D," said Haas, "with matte painting only for the very far backgrounds. Shading and lighting for the Washington D.C. shots was supervised by 3D lead Alex Hupperich, while Tobias Gerdts was compositing lead. The crowd erupts into panic when the massive mothership appears overhead and prepares to land, darkening skies over North America, Europe and Asia. Scanline delivered 150 shots of the mothership's arrival, including those in which the ship sets down in Washington D.C., Singapore, London and the Gulf of Mexico. Opening shots in the arrival sequence harkened back to the original Independence Day. "In that movie," recalled Bryan Grill, "you first see the alien ship appear through a cloud. When we started on this movie, we looked at that, and wondered what it was. Was it an actual cloud? Was it just some phenomenon generated from the alien ship? And then, talking with Volker, we learned that when the ship enters the Earth's atmosphere it starts to burn, and all of this smoke comes off of it. They had created that look, originally, by shooting cloud tank elements. We had to replicate that beautiful cloud tank work using Flowline, which became a big development task for us." "Even though the technology was different," added Scanline Vancouver visual effects supervisor Mohsen Mousavi, Roland wanted us to re-create those iconic shots of the destroyer coming out of the cloud. We had all fallen in love with those shots 20 years ago, and we wanted to keep their look and feel, even though we were creating them digitally 17 / 33 through some mind-blowing simulations instead of practical cloud tank photography."

INDEPENDENCE DAY Scanline founder and senior visual effects supervisor Stephan Trojansky oversaw the Flowline effects simulation work, along with visual effects supervisor Julius Lechner. Scale, again, presented the most pressing technical challenge.iWe had to push the boundaries to be able to simulate this at such a huge scale," Mousavi noted. With more than 100 million user accounts created since the game's inception, it was only a matter of time before the warriors of this interactive fantasy world received their call-up papers to continue the campaign onto the big screen. Blizzard and Legendary Pictures first announced their intention to adapt the Warcraft series of games as a feature film in 2006. But it was not until 2013, following early development and the departure of original director Sam Raimi, that the project finally hit its stride. Duncan Jones would direct Legendary's and Universal Pictures' Warcraft from a script written by himself and Charles Leavitt, based on a story by Blizzard's senior vice president of creative development, Chris Metzen. Lord of the Apes BY JOE FORDHAM E Idgar Rice Burroughs' 1912 novel, Tarzan of the Apes, captured readers' imaginations - literary critics surmised - by tapping into the early 20th Century zeitgeist of Darwinian discoveries and colonialism. The story, about the orphaned son of a shipwrecked English nobleman who is born into the jungles of Africa and raised by apes, spawned more than two dozen further adventures, including Burroughs' stories published posthumously. Hollywood adaptations appeared as early as 1915, with a silent movie starring Elmo Lincoln, followed by a parade of jungle he-men including Buster Crabbe and Johnny Weissmuller. The 1980s saw Miles O'Keeffe play Tarzan as second fiddle to his Amazonian mate in a vehicle for Bo Derek; while Christopher Lambert provided a more thoughtful take on the role in Greystoke: The Legend of Tarzan, Lord of the Apes, co-starring Rick Baker's spectacular animatronic apes. Walt Disney's 1999 animated Tarzan emphasized the character's tree-surfing abilities. Arguably, the most faithful adaptation of Burroughs' jungle hero had yet to be realized, and in the early 2000s Warner Bros. investigated a new production with potential 1 / 31| directors Guillermo del Toro and Stephen Sommers. Director David Yates was drawn to V

TARZAN the project after proving his mettle with the final four Harry Potter films.iThere was something about a human being caught between two worlds that I found compellingi commented Yates. ¿The notion of this man who has a primal start to life and who is then expected to slot into his role as an English lord presented a fascinating conflict. Hoved the idea of a character that was not a superhero, but has extraordinary skills that give him an ability to commune with nature. The script that Adam Cozad and Craig Brewer wrote contained a lot of themes that I felt were relevant to our century, including the notion of how we interact with our environment, why we have to protect our environment and the animals within it. For all those reasons, I felt it was time to give Tarzan and the world in which he exists a bigger stage because the themes and the character deserved it. The Legend of Tarzan introduces Tarzan (Alexander Skarsgard) as Lord John Clayton, residing in Greystoke Manor in Victorian England, until an American politician, Captain George Washington Williams (Samuel L. Jackson), persuades him to return to the Belgian Congo. In the African township of Boma, Tarzan and Williams discover Léon Rom (Christoph Waltz), a captain of the Belgian colonial militia, pillaging the jungle for its natural resources. A rivalry evolves when Rom kidnaps Tarzan's wife, Jane Porter (Margot Robbie), as part of a pact with a local tribal chief, M' bonga (Djimon Hounsou), sworn enemy of Tarzan, and guardian of a cache of diamonds. While attempting to rescue Jane, Tarzan revisits his animalistic origins and comes to terms with his place as Lord of the Apes.
